title: Repair bills that grew after the purchase
question: Once the City had bought or funded a building for homeless housing, did the repair estimate hold?
finding: The Budget and Legislative Analyst counted 8 homeless-housing sites approved since 2020–21 that cost $395,650,000 to buy, before repairs. For the two it re-checked, repairs rose from $15,602,150 to $85,309,595, $69,707,445 more (447%); at 1000 Sutter Street the estimate went from $6,540,000 to $67,459,595.
how: Exhibits 3.3 and 3.4 of the audit, read from the text of the report. Where the State’s Homekey award list covers the building and counts its homes differently, the State’s count is used for the per-home figures and the audit’s count is shown beside it. The audit says site inspections before purchase covered immediate repair needs and accessibility but not building systems, hazardous materials or ground conditions. “All in” adds the latest repair figure the audit gives to the purchase price.
limits: These are the auditor’s figures as of May 2024, not final costs. The audit faults the estimates, not the sellers or operators; it notes that unforeseen conditions are always possible in old buildings. Two of the eight (440 Geary and 1000 Sutter) were bought by a nonprofit with State and City money rather than by the City itself.

columns.t: Homes (State Homekey list where it has the building)

rows.countNote: The State’s Homekey Round 2 award list gives 170 units (168 assisted) for City Gardens; the audit’s Exhibit 3.3 gives 200. Per-home figures use the State’s count.
The State’s Homekey Round 2 award list gives 51 units (50 assisted) for Mission Inn; the audit’s Exhibit 3.3 gives 52. Per-home figures use the State’s count.

sources.t: Budget and Legislative Analyst, Performance Audit of Permanent Supportive Housing Funds (3 May 2024), Exhibits 3.3 and 3.4
